冬不拉出現在哈薩克、哈扎拉、烏茲別克、塔吉克、諾蓋、巴什基爾與韃靼傳統音樂，也用: The dombra appears in the traditional music of Kazakhstan, the Hazara, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, the Nogai, the Bashkirs and the Tatars, and is also used in state ceremonies and large public performances. In Kazakh music it accompanies the narrative song (jir) and plays the solo küy; the western tökpe and eastern shertpe schools are linked with names such as Kurmangazy Sagyrbaiuly and Tattimbet Kazangapuly. The Hazara and Tajiks of Afghanistan use it to accompany sung verse, the Bashkirs to accompany epic singers; today it is also heard in the electric version used by folk-rock bands.
冬不拉琴身傳統以松、雲杉或杏木整塊製成，面板薄而平或微拱，背板可整塊雕刻或以彎貼: The dombra's body is traditionally made from a single block of pine, spruce or apricot, with a thin flat or slightly arched soundboard, and a back that is either carved from the solid or built up from bent staves; the frets on the neck were once tied on with gut or sinew and are now mostly nylon line or fixed metal. The strings were once sinew or twisted gut, now mostly nylon. The fretless types, such as those of the Afghan Hazara, carve the body and neck from a single piece of mulberry or apricot, with a thick wooden soundboard, a small soundhole in the back, usually no varnish, and decoration only in inlay or pokerwork.

The dombra is a long-necked plucked lute, the chief national instrument of Kazakhstan, and is also found in the traditional music of the Hazara, Uzbeks, Tajiks, the Nogai, the Bashkirs and the Tatars. The standard Kazakh type has a pear-shaped or elongated triangular soundbox, a slender neck and two strings, the neck carrying movable frets and the strings mostly nylon. Playing divides into western strumming and eastern plucking, and the soundboard can be struck; it is used to accompany songs, for solo küy and in state ceremonies. Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-6.
哈薩克冬不拉以兩弦撥奏發聲，低弦常作持續音，高弦奏旋律。音量與音色以右手技法控制: The Kazakh dombra sounds from its two plucked strings, the low string often a drone and the high one carrying the melody. Volume and timbre are controlled by the right hand: strumming makes both strings sound together and is more percussive; single plucking with fingertip and nail sounds each string, is more lyrical and less percussive, and the soundboard can be tapped for extra rhythm. The range varies with the number of frets: eight or nine are usual for accompanying songs, and complex tunes reach eighteen to twenty-four. Compared with long-necked lutes of the same family, the Afghan dambura is fretless, has a small soundhole in the back and more often uses the soundboard for percussion.

類似冬不拉的長頸兩弦撥弦魯特琴，見於中世紀中亞草原與綠洲文化；Al-Farabi: A long-necked two-string plucked lute similar to the dombra is found in the medieval nomadic and oasis cultures of Central Asia; Al-Farabi (c. 872–950) mentions long-necked lutes in Khorasan and Baghdad. The Kazakh classical repertoire took shape in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, passed on orally from master to pupil by named player-composers, with the western strumming and eastern plucking schools side by side. The Bashkir dombra once accompanied epic singing, was lost at some point between the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and was rebuilt and revived in the second half of the twentieth. The Kazakh art of the solo küy was inscribed on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2014.
